Title: CSRF Protection Weakened or Disabled
Description:
Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) is a type of vulnerability where
attacker tricks user into submitting  a state change on
the server, such as changing the user's password via attacker's site. If the
web application relies only on cookies for authentication, or on other
credentials that are automatically included in the request, then this
request will appear as legitimate to the server.
Examples:
MIDDLEWARE = [
    'django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware',
    'django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware',
    'django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware',
    # 'django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware',
    'django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware',
    'django.contrib.messages.middleware.MessageMiddleware',
    'django.middleware.clickjacking.XFrameOptionsMiddleware',
]

Title: Using Broken or Weak Cryptographic Hashing Algorithm On Sensitive Data
Description:
Using a broken or weak cryptographic hash function can leave sensitive data
like passwords and certificates
vulnerable to attacks. As an example, both MD5 and SHA-1 are 
known to be vulnerable to attacks.
Examples:
import hashlib

def certificate_matches_known_hash_bad(certificate, known_hash):
    hash = hashlib.md5(certificate).hexdigest() # BAD
    return hash == known_hash

def certificate_matches_known_hash_good(certificate, known_hash):
    hash = hashlib.sha256(certificate).hexdigest() # GOOD
    return hash == known_hash
$$$
import hashlib

def get_password_hash(password: str, salt: str):
    return hashlib.sha256(password + salt).hexdigest() # BAD
$$$
from argon2 import PasswordHasher

def get_initial_hash(password: str):
    ph = PasswordHasher()
    return ph.hash(password) # GOOD

def check_password(password: str, known_hash):
    ph = PasswordHasher()
    return ph.verify(known_hash, password) # GOOD

Title: Incomplete Regular Expression for Hostnames
Description:
Sanitizing untrusted URLs is common for preventing attacks by checking that
the host of a URL is in the set of allowed hosts. If a regex implements such
checks,being too permissive by not escaping '.' meta-characters can lead to
code vulnerabilities.

Title: Deserialization of User-Controlled Data
Description:
Automatic deserialization of fields means that an attacker may
craft a nested combination of objects on which the executed initialization code
may have unforeseen effects, such as the execution of arbitrary code.
Deserialization libraries like Pickle, Marshal and Yaml are vulnerable to this attack.

Description:
With higher computation, cryptographic algorithms can be broken.
If the key sizes of algorithms RSA and DSA are less than 2048 bits and
for ECC if it is less than 256 bits, then the cryptographic key is vulnerable
to attacks.

Title: SQL Query Built From User-Controlled Sources
Description:
If SQL query is built from
user-provided data without checks, a user
can run malicious queries.
Examples:
from django.conf.urls import url
from django.db import connection


def show_user(request, username):
    with connection.cursor() as cursor:
        # BAD -- Using string formatting
        cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '%s'" % username)
        user = cursor.fetchone()

        # GOOD -- Using parameters
        cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = %s", username)
        user = cursor.fetchone()

        # BAD -- Manually quoting placeholder (%s)
        cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '%s'", username)
        user = cursor.fetchone()

urlpatterns = [url(r'^users/(?P<username>[^/]+)$', show_user)]

Title: Server-Side Request Forgery
Description:
Directly using user input into an HTTP request without validation
can facilitate server-side request forgery (SSRF) attacks. In these attacks, the
request may be changed, directed at a different server, or via a different
protocol. This can allow the attacker to obtain sensitive information or perform
actions with escalated privilege.We make a distinctions between 
how much of the URL an attacker can control:
-Full SSRF: where the full URL can be controlled.
-Partial SSRF: where only part of the URL can be controlled, such as the
path component of a URL to a hardcoded domain.
Examples:
import requests
from flask import Flask, request

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/full_ssrf")
def full_ssrf():
    target = request.args["target"]

    # BAD: user has full control of URL
    resp = requests.get("https://" + target + ".example.com/data/")

    # GOOD: `subdomain` is controlled by the server.
    subdomain = "europe" if target == "EU" else "world"
    resp = requests.get("https://" + subdomain + ".example.com/data/")
$$$
import requests
from flask import Flask, request

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/partial_ssrf")
def partial_ssrf():
    user_id = request.args["user_id"]

    # BAD: user can fully control the path component of the URL
    resp = requests.get("https://api.example.com/user_info/" + user_id)

    if user_id.isalnum():
        # GOOD: user_id is restricted to be alpha-numeric, and cannot alter path component of URL
        resp = requests.get("https://api.example.com/user_info/" + user_id)

Title: Arbitrary File Write During Tarfile Extraction
Description:
Tar archives contain entries where each entry
include a file path. These paths may not be restricted  contain
unexpected special elements like '..' for traversal. This might lead to files
written in unexpected location or sensitive information mishandled. For example, 
if a tar archive contains a file entry '..\sneaky-file;, and the tar archive
is extracted to 'c:\output', then naively combining the paths would result
in an output file path of 'c:\output\..\sneaky-file', which would cause the file to be
written to 'c:\sneaky-file'.
Examples:
import sys
import tarfile

with tarfile.open(sys.argv[1]) as tar:
    #BAD : This could write any file on the filesystem.
    for entry in tar:
        tar.extract(entry, "/tmp/unpack/")
$$$
import sys
import tarfile
import os.path

with tarfile.open(sys.argv[1]) as tar:
    for entry in tar:
        #GOOD: Check that entry is safe
        if os.path.isabs(entry.name) or ".." in entry.name:
            raise ValueError("Illegal tar archive entry")
        tar.extract(entry, "/tmp/unpack/")

Title: NoSQL Injection
Description:
Passing user-controlled sources into NoSQL queries can result in a NoSQL injection flaw.
This tainted NoSQL query containing a user-controlled source can then 
execute a malicious query in a NoSQL database such as MongoDB.
In order for the user-controlled source to taint the NoSQL 
query, the user-controller source must be converted into a 
Python object using something like 'json.loads' or 'xmltodict.parse'

Title: Request Without Certificate Validation
Description:
Disabling the encryption certificate verification that TLS provides can create security issues.
Functions in the 'requests' module provide verification by default. It is only when
explicitly turned off using 'verify=False' that no verification occurs.
Examples:
import requests

#Unsafe requests

requests.get('https://semmle.com', verify=False) # UNSAFE
requests.get('https://semmle.com', verify=0) # UNSAFE

#Various safe options

requests.get('https://semmle.com', verify=True) # Explicitly safe
requests.get('https://semmle.com', verify="/path/to/cert/")
requests.get('https://semmle.com') # The default is to verify.

#Wrapper to ensure safety

def make_safe_request(url, verify_cert):
    if not verify_cert:
        raise Exception("Trying to make unsafe request")
    return requests.get(url, verify_cert)

to take a very long time or use large amounts of memory, resulting in an XML bomb attack.
For instance, in 'lxml' library, if 'huge_tree' is set to 'True', it could result in this issue.

and include user input without any validation, user can run malicious LDAP queries.
If such queries are not escaped using functions like 'ldap.dn.escape_dn_chars'
or 'ldap.filter.escape_filter_chars', 'ldap3.utils.dn.escape_rdn' or

    ldap_connection = ldap.initialize("ldap://127.0.0.1")
    user = ldap_connection.search_s(
        dn, ldap.SCOPE_SUBTREE, search_filter)

Title: Incomplete URL Substring Sanitization
Description:
Sanitizing untrusted URLs is common for preventing attacks by checking that
the host of a URL is in the set of allowed hosts. However, treating the URL as a 
string and checking if one of the allowed hosts is a substring of 
the URL is prone to errors. Malicious URLs can bypass such security checks 
by embedding one of the allowed hosts in an unexpected location

Description:
An external API is defined as a call to a method that is not defined in the source
code, and is not modeled as a taint step in the default taint library. As such 
providing unsanitized data or user input to such APIs can result in a variety of security issues.

Title: Polynomial Regular Expression Used On Uncontrolled Data
Description:
Consider this use of a regular expression, which removes
all leading and trailing whitespace in a string:
re.sub(r"^\s+|\s+$", "", text).The sub-expression '"\s+$"' will match the
whitespace characters in 'text' from left to right, but it
can start matching anywhere within a whitespace sequence. This is
problematic for strings that do not end with a whitespace
character. Such a string will force the regular expression engine to
process each whitespace sequence once per whitespace character in the
sequence. This ultimately means that the time cost of trimming a
string is quadratic in the length of the string. So a string like
'"a b"' will take milliseconds to process, but a similar
string with a million spaces instead of just one will take several
minutes. Without using a negative look-behind
('^\s+|(?<!\s)\s+$'), or using the built-in strip
method ('text.strip()'), this problem is unavoidable.

Title: Default Version of SSL/TLS May Be Insecure
Description:
'ssl.wrap_socket' function defaults to an insecure version of SSL/TLS, leaving the connection 
vulnerable to attack. All versions of SSL, and TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are 
known to be vulnerable to attacks.
If no explicit 'ssl_version' is specified, the default 'PROTOCOL_TLS' 
is chosen. This protocol is insecure because it allows TLS 1.0 and 
TLS 1.1 and so should not be used.
Examples:
import ssl
import socket

# Using the deprecated ssl.wrap_socket method
ssl.wrap_socket(socket.socket(), ssl_version=ssl.PROTOCOL_SSLv2)

# Using SSLContext
context = ssl.SSLContext(ssl_version=ssl.PROTOCOL_SSLv3)

# Using pyOpenSSL

from pyOpenSSL import SSL

context = SSL.Context(SSL.TLSv1_METHOD)


$$$

context.options |= ssl.OP_NO_TLSv1 | ssl.OP_NO_TLSv1_1

Title: XML External Entity Expansion
Description:
Parsing untrusted XML files with a weakly configured XML parser may lead to an
XML External Entity (XXE) attack. If external entity handling is not disabled when
parsing untrusted data, then this attack can happen.

Title: Jinja2 Templating With Autoescape = False
Description:
XSS attacks can occur if untrusted input is not escaped. 
This applies to templates as well as code.
Jinja2 templates may be vulnerable to XSS attacks if the environment has 
'autoescape' set to 'False'. Unfortunately, 'jinja2' sets 'autoescape' 
to 'False' by default. Explicitly setting 'autoescape' to 'True' when creating an 
'Environment' object will prevent this.

Title: Creating A Temporary File May Be Insecure
Description:
Functions that create temporary file names (such as 'tempfile.mktemp'
and 'os.tempnam') are fundamentally insecure, as they do not
ensure exclusive access to a file with the temporary name they return.
The file name returned by these functions is guaranteed to be unique on
creation but the file must be opened in a separate operation. There is no
guarantee that the creation and open operations will happen atomically. This
provides an opportunity for an attacker to interfere with the file before it is
opened.
Examples:
from tempfile import mktemp

def write_results(results):
    filename = mktemp()
    with open(filename, "w+") as f:
        f.write(results)
    print("Results written to", filename)
$$$
from tempfile import NamedTemporaryFile

def write_results(results):
    with NamedTemporaryFile(mode="w+", delete=False) as f:
        f.write(results)
    print("Results written to", f.name)

Title: Accepting Unknown SSH Host Keys When Using Paramiko
Description: In SSH protocol, host keys are used to verify the identity of remote hosts. Accepting unknown host keys may leave the connection open to man-in-the-middle attacks. In particular, setting the default missing host key policy for the Paramiko library to either 'AutoAddPolicy' or 'WarningPolicy'' continue even with unknown hosts.
Examples:
from paramiko.client import SSHClient, AutoAddPolicy, RejectPolicy

def unsafe_connect():
    client = SSHClient()
    client.set_missing_host_key_policy(AutoAddPolicy)
    client.connect("example.com")

    # ... interaction with server

    client.close()

def safe_connect():
    client = SSHClient()
    client.set_missing_host_key_policy(RejectPolicy)
    client.connect("example.com")

    # ... interaction with server

    client.close()

Title: PAM Authorization Bypass Due To Incorrect Usage
Description:
Using only a call to 'pam_authenticate' to check the validity of a login can lead to 
authorization bypass vulnerabilities. A 'pam_authenticate'
only verifies the credentials of a user. It does not check if a user has an
appropriate authorization to actually login. This means a user with an expired
login or a password can still access the system.
Examples:
libpam                    = CDLL(find_library("pam"))

pam_authenticate          = libpam.pam_authenticate
pam_authenticate.restype  = c_int
pam_authenticate.argtypes = [PamHandle, c_int]

def authenticate(username, password, service='login'):
    def my_conv(n_messages, messages, p_response, app_data):
        """
        Simple conversation function that responds to any prompt where the echo is off with the supplied password
        """
        ...

    handle = PamHandle()
    conv   = PamConv(my_conv, 0)
    retval = pam_start(service, username, byref(conv), byref(handle))

    retval = pam_authenticate(handle, 0)
    return retval == 0
$$$
libpam                    = CDLL(find_library("pam"))

pam_authenticate          = libpam.pam_authenticate
pam_authenticate.restype  = c_int
pam_authenticate.argtypes = [PamHandle, c_int]

pam_acct_mgmt          = libpam.pam_acct_mgmt
pam_acct_mgmt.restype  = c_int
pam_acct_mgmt.argtypes = [PamHandle, c_int]

def authenticate(username, password, service='login'):
    def my_conv(n_messages, messages, p_response, app_data):
        """
        Simple conversation function that responds to any prompt where the echo is off with the supplied password
        """
        ...

    handle = PamHandle()
    conv   = PamConv(my_conv, 0)
    retval = pam_start(service, username, byref(conv), byref(handle))

    retval = pam_authenticate(handle, 0)
    if retval == 0:
        retval = pam_acct_mgmt(handle, 0)
    return retval == 0

Title: Log Injection
Description:
If unsanitized user input is written to a log entry, 
a malicious user may be able to forge new log entries.
Forgery can occur if a user provides some input with characters that are interpreted
when the log output is displayed. If the log is displayed as a plain text file, then new
line characters can be used by a malicious user to create the appearance of multiple log
entries. If the log is displayed as HTML, then arbitrary HTML may be included to spoof
log entries.
Examples:
#!/usr/bin/env python
# -*- coding: UTF-8 -*-
"""
@Desc   ：Log Injection
"""
from flask import Flask
from flask import request
from django.utils.log import request_logger
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/bad1')
def bad1():
    name = request.args.get('name')
    app.logger.info('User name: ' + name) # Bad
    return 'bad1'

@app.route('/bad2')
def bad2():
    name = request.args.get('name')
    logging.info('User name: ' + name) # Bad
    return 'bad2'

@app.route('/bad3')
def bad3():
    name = request.args.get('name')
    request_logger.warn('User name: ' + name) # Bad
    return 'bad3'

@app.route('/bad4')
def bad4():
    name = request.args.get('name')

    logtest.debug('User name: ' + name) # Bad
    return 'bad4'

if __name__ == '__main__':
    app.debug = True
    handler = logging.FileHandler('log')
    app.logger.addHandler(handler)
    app.run()

Using broken or weak cryptographic algorithms can leave data
vulnerable to being decrypted or forged by an attacker. Any

Title: Code Injection
Description:
Directly evaluating user input (for example, an HTTP request parameter) 
as code without properly sanitizing the input first allows an attacker 
arbitrary code execution. This can occur when user
input is passed to code that interprets it as an expression to be
evaluated, such as 'eval' or 'exec'.

Title: Unsafe Shell Command Constructed From Library Input
Description:
Dynamically constructing shell commands with inputs from library 
functions may  change the meaning of the commands.
Clients may use inputs containing characters that the shell interprets in a 
special way, for instance quotes and spaces.
This can result in the shell command misbehaving or malicious actor control of system.

Title: Hard-Coded Credentials
Description:
Hard-coding credentials, such as username, password and certificates, instead of saving
them in configuration files or encrypting them during transmission can result in 
attackers discovering sensitive information.
Examples:
import hashlib
import binascii

def process_request(request):
    password = request.GET["password"]

    # BAD: Inbound authentication made by comparison to string literal
    if password == "myPa55word":
        redirect("login")

    hashed_password = load_from_config('hashed_password', CONFIG_FILE)
    salt = load_from_config('salt', CONFIG_FILE)

    #GOOD: Inbound authentication made by comparing to a hash password from a config file.
    dk = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac('sha256', password, salt, 100000)
    hashed_input = binascii.hexlify(dk)
    if hashed_input == hashed_password:
        redirect("login")

Title: Information Exposure Through An Exception
Description:
Developers utilize error stack trace to fix bugs. However, attackers can also
use information from stack trace. The sequence of class names in a stack trace 
can reveal the structure
of the application as well as any internal components it relies on.
Error message at the top of a stack trace can include
information such as server-side file names and application SQL code, 
allowing an attacker to fine-tune a subsequent injection attack.

Title: Bad HTML Tag Filtering
Description:
If poor regex is used for HTML tag filtering, it can lead to XSS attacks or other
security issues. They are caused by browsers with forgiving HTML parsers, and
will often render invalid HTML containing syntax errors. 
Regex should also recognize tags containing such syntax errors.
Examples:
import re

def filterScriptTags(content): 
    oldContent = ""
    while oldContent != content:
        oldContent = content
        content = re.sub(r'<script.*?>.*?</script>', '', content, flags= re.DOTALL | re.IGNORECASE)
    return content

Title: Clear-text Storage of Sensitive Information
Description:
Sensitive information stored unencrypted is accessible to an attacker
who gains access to the storage. This is particularly important for cookies,
which are stored on the machine of the end-user.
Examples:

Title: URL Redirection From Remote Source
Description:
Using user input for URL redirection without validation poses security risks 
like phishing attacks by redirecting to an attacker's website.

Title: Uncontrolled Command Line
Description:
Code that passes user input directly to 'exec', 'eval', or some other library
routine that executes a command, allows the user to execute malicious
code.

Title: Overly Permissive Regular Expression Range
Description:
It's easy to write a regular expression range that matches a wider range of 
characters than you intended. For example, '/[a-zA-z]/' matches all 
lowercase and all uppercase letters,as you would expect, 
but it also matches the characters: '[ \ ] ^ _ `'. Another common problem is 
failing to escape the dash character in a regular expression. An unescaped dash is 
interpreted as part of a range. For example, in the character class 
'[a-zA-Z0-9%=.,-_]' the last character range matches the 55 characters 
between ',' and '_' (both included), which overlaps with the range 
'[0-9]' and is clearly not intended by the writer.

Title: Uncontrolled Data Used In Path Expression
Description:
File access via user input can allow attackers to access sensitive
data and modify files. Some examples of how this issue can occur are: 
- allowing more than a single '.' character
- allowing separators such as '/' or '\'
- relying on simply replacing problematic sequences such as '../'
Examples:
import os.path
from flask import Flask, request, abort

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/user_picture1")
def user_picture1():
    filename = request.args.get('p')
    # BAD: This could read any file on the file system
    data = open(filename, 'rb').read()
    return data

@app.route("/user_picture2")
def user_picture2():
    base_path = '/server/static/images'
    filename = request.args.get('p')
    # BAD: This could still read any file on the file system
    data = open(os.path.join(base_path, filename), 'rb').read()
